covers.quote: The word ‘disinterested’ means ‘impartial’ and ‘unbiased by personal interest’.
The word ‘uninterested’ means ‘not interested’, ‘indifferent’ or ‘unconcerned’.

parts.quote: The judge’s deliberation was disinterested and considered.
The invitation to the concert was wasted on me because I’m uninterested in jazz music.

rules.quote: ‘Disinterested’ is often used to mean ‘uninterested’, but this use is not correct.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Disinterested’ is used to mean not interested, indifferent or unconcerned, rather than impartial or unbiased.
when: Applies when ‘disinterested’ expresses a lack of interest.
Use meaning impartial or unbiased by personal interest is not a violation.
rules.why: G-4: the explicit prohibition supplies the rule; the definitions explain its scope rather than creating additional rules.

covers.quote: The word ‘dove’ is the past tense of ‘dive’ in American English.

parts.quote: Bystanders dived into the creek to help the drowning swimmer.

rules.quote: In Australian English, write ‘dived’ to use the past tense of the verb ‘to dive’.
rules.violation_condition: The past tense of the verb ‘dive’ is written as ‘dove’ in Australian English.
when: Applies to the past tense of the verb ‘dive’ in Australian English.
Does not apply to ‘dove’ as the name of a bird.
rules.why: G-4: use the body instruction, not the topical heading or the description of American English.

covers.quote: for all intents and purposes/for all intensive purposes

parts.quote: The paperwork may take a few weeks to come through but, for all intents and purposes, you are hired.

rules.quote: The correct expression is ‘for all intents and purposes’, meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.violation_condition: The expression ‘for all intensive purposes’ is used instead of ‘for all intents and purposes’.
when: Applies to the expression meaning ‘in every practical sense’.
rules.why: G-4: the body identifies the correct expression; the heading identifies the competing forms.

covers.quote: The exception is a court decision; write this as ‘judgment’.

parts.quote: You can speak to one of our counsellors without fearing judgement.
Please cite the High Court’s most recent judgment in the issues paper.

rules.violation_condition: ‘Judgment’ is used outside the court-decision sense, or ‘judgement’ is used for a court decision.
when: The general spelling is ‘judgement’.
For a court decision, the spelling is ‘judgment’.
rules.why: G-2: the court-decision exception changes which spelling is appropriate, not the underlying spelling check.

parts.quote: He completed his master degree last year.
The university offered several master degrees to postgraduate students.

rules.violation_condition: A generic reference to a master degree is written as ‘masters degree’ or ‘master’s degree’.
when: Applies to generic references to this level of degree, including plural ‘master degrees’.
Specific qualifications are covered by the separate ‘Master of [area of study]’ instruction.
rules.why: The grain test separates the generic spelling check from the check on the form of a specific qualification’s name.

parts.quote: Having a Master of Arts helped her gain the promotion.

rules.quote: When referring to a specific qualification, use ‘Master of [area of study]’.
rules.violation_condition: A specific master qualification is named in a form other than ‘Master of’ followed by its area of study.
when: Applies when naming a specific qualification, rather than referring generically to a master degree.
rules.why: The grain test keeps qualification naming separate from the generic ‘master degree’ spelling check.

covers.quote: Use ‘program’ for the titles of new programs based on government policy.
Use ‘programme’ only when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.

parts.quote: One of the most challenging aspects of our work is designing programs that can be implemented quickly.
The Prescription Shopping Programme lets medical practitioners check their patients’ prescription histories.

rules.quote: Use ‘program’ rather than ‘programme’, including for computer programs.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Programme’ is used outside the formal name of an existing program, including in a newly created government-policy program title.
when: Applies to ordinary uses, computer programs and titles of new programs based on government policy.
‘Programme’ is allowed when it is part of the formal name of an existing program.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: ordinary uses, new titles and the existing-name exception belong to one spelling check.

covers.quote: It is not accepted as standard Australian English.

parts.quote: Our aim is for all staff to have access to this training, regardless of location.
The following instructions will work regardless of which mobile platform you use.
These are interesting times but we must carry on regardless.

rules.why: G-4: the instruction and the statement that ‘irregardless’ is non-standard support one check.

covers.quote: would have/would of
‘Would of’ is incorrect.

parts.quote: If I had known we were over budget, I would have changed the scope of the contract.
This would’ve spared us a lot of stress
At the very least, we would of avoided the overspend.

rules.quote: Always write ‘would have’ or the contracted form ‘would’ve’.
rules.violation_condition: ‘Would of’ is used in place of the verb form ‘would have’ or ‘would’ve’.
when: Both ‘would have’ and ‘would’ve’ are acceptable.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the full and contracted forms are alternatives within one check; the incorrectness statement is a restatement.
